title: Enterprise Data and ML Platforms
subtitle: Architect data lakes, lakehouses, streaming pipelines, hybrid cloud deployments and governed MLOps for an enterprise, and build working miniatures of each on your laptop.
outcomes: Architect a scalable, zoned data lake with incremental, idempotent ingestion
Design lakehouse tables with ACID transactions, time travel and query optimisation, and explain how Delta Lake and Apache Iceberg work
Design streaming pipelines with event-time windows, watermarks, state and real-time features for ML
Construct hybrid cloud ML systems with reliable synchronisation, portable deployment, security and compliance
Establish enterprise MLOps with maturity assessments, continuous training and governed model promotion
prerequisites: Python, SQL and the ML workflow from training to deployment; Foundations of AI System Design and Data Engineering Foundations: Batch and Streaming Pipelines are good preparation. Install Python 3.10 or newer, then: pip install pandas numpy scikit-learn duckdb pyarrow. The optional Delta Lake steps add pip install deltalake. Everything runs locally on sample data: no cloud account is needed.
description:
Enterprises rarely struggle to train a model; they struggle to give it trustworthy data at the right speed, run it in the places their data and rules allow, and prove later what it did and why. This course is about the platforms that make that possible. You'll learn why organisations modernise from scattered databases and warehouses, how a zoned data lake is organised and fed, how lakehouse table formats such as Delta Lake and Apache Iceberg add ACID transactions and time travel to files in object storage, how stream processors handle late and duplicated events with event-time windows and watermarks, how hybrid architectures keep data and models consistent across on-premises sites and clouds under residency and privacy rules, and how enterprise MLOps automates retraining while keeping humans accountable.

The labs follow a hydropower company's turbine data, and each builds a working miniature of a platform component on your laptop with Python, DuckDB and SQLite: a raw, clean and curated lake with incremental ingestion and late corrections; a small table format with a transaction log, optimistic concurrency, time travel, data skipping, compaction and vacuum, compared with a real Delta Lake log; a stream processor with watermarks and a real-time feature checked against batch SQL; cross-environment synchronisation with reconciliation, pseudonymisation and policy checks; and a governed retraining gate with a registry and audit log. The capstone is a cloud-agnostic lakehouse and MLOps architecture, documented with a diagram and decision records and backed by a runnable walking skeleton.

modules.title: Modernisation Strategy and Data Lakes
modules.summary: Why organisations modernise their data platforms, how a zoned data lake is organised, how to design its storage layer, and how data gets in: full, incremental, change data capture and streaming ingestion.

lessons.title: Why organisations modernise their data platforms
objectives: Identify the drivers of data platform modernisation
Plan an incremental migration with measurable outcomes
key_points: Common drivers are data locked in departmental databases, warehouses that can't hold semi-structured or high-volume data cheaply, batch reports that arrive too late for operational decisions, and ML teams copying extracts by hand.
Modernise incrementally: move the highest-value use cases first and run old and new side by side, retiring the old piece by piece (the strangler fig approach), rather than one big-bang migration.

Separate storage from compute: open formats on object storage (Amazon S3, Azure Data Lake Storage, Google Cloud Storage or an S3-compatible store on site) let several engines share one copy of the data and scale independently.
Make the case with measurable outcomes: time from event to insight, manual extracts retired, data quality incidents, and the cost of running each pipeline.

Plan the operating model as well as the technology: who owns each dataset, what the platform team provides, and how governance works. Data mesh, for example, makes domains own their data as products on a shared self-service platform.

lessons.title: Data lake architecture and zones
objectives: Describe a zoned (medallion) data lake
Explain what keeps a lake from becoming a swamp
key_points: A data lake stores raw and processed data of any kind as files in scalable object storage, applying a schema when data is read (schema-on-read) rather than when it is loaded.

Zones separate trust levels: raw (bronze) keeps data as received, append-only, for replay and audit; clean (silver) is typed, deduplicated and validated; curated (gold) holds aggregates and features. This layering is often called the medallion architecture.
Quarantine records that fail validation instead of dropping them silently, so they can be inspected, fixed at the source and replayed.

A catalog, such as Hive Metastore, AWS Glue Data Catalog, Unity Catalog or an Apache Iceberg REST catalog, records each table's schema, location, owner and access rules, so data can be found and governed.
Without ownership, a catalog, quality checks and retention rules, a lake becomes a data swamp: files nobody can find, trust or safely delete.

lessons.title: Designing the storage layer
objectives: Choose formats, layout and partitioning for a lake
Plan retention, lifecycle and access by zone
key_points: Use open columnar formats such as Parquet for analytics, with compression; keep raw copies in the format received when replaying them matters.
Partition by what most queries filter on, often a date, at a grain that keeps files large: every small file costs a request and metadata work, so compact small files into bigger ones.
Object stores aren't file systems: listing large prefixes is slow and many lack an atomic rename, so a correct table shouldn't depend on directory listings; that's part of why table formats exist.
Lay out paths predictably (zone, domain, table, partition=value) and record them in the catalog; use lifecycle rules to move old data to cheaper storage classes and delete what retention allows.
Encrypt data at rest and grant access by zone and table: far fewer people need raw data than curated data.

lessons.title: Ingestion strategies
objectives: Compare full, incremental, change data capture and streaming ingestion
Make ingestion idempotent
key_points: Full snapshot ingestion copies the whole source table each time: simple and robust, but expensive for large tables, and it can't tell what changed.
Incremental ingestion copies rows changed since a high-watermark, such as the largest updated_at already loaded; it is cheap, but it misses hard deletes and trusts the watermark column completely.
Change data capture (CDC) reads the database's own change log, for example with Debezium, and emits every insert, update and delete in order, with little load on the source.
Make ingestion idempotent: write each batch as an immutable file named by its range, and advance the watermark only after the write succeeds, so a retry never loses or duplicates data.
Streaming ingestion lands events continuously from a log such as Apache Kafka. Batch and streaming usually coexist, with the raw zone as their shared landing place.

lab.title: Build a zoned data lake with incremental ingestion

lab.submit: Paste your lake.py, the output of each run, and your design note.

files.content:
"""Create plant.db, a SQLite stand-in for a hydropower plant's operational database.

python make_plant_db.py         three days of turbine readings (with a few sensor glitches)
python make_plant_db.py --day4  add the fourth day's readings and correct three earlier ones
Fixed seed: everyone gets the same rows."""

import sqlite3
import sys
from datetime import datetime, timedelta

import numpy as np

START = datetime(2025, 6, 1)


def readings(rng, first_day, days):
    rows = []
    for d in range(first_day, first_day + days):
        for slot in range(48):                                  # every 30 minutes
            t = START + timedelta(days=d, minutes=30 * slot)
            for turbine in ["T1", "T2", "T3", "T4"]:
                vibration = round(float(rng.normal(3.0 + (0.8 if turbine == "T4" else 0), 0.4)), 2)
                if rng.rand() < 0.004:
                    vibration = 999.0                           # a sensor glitch
                rows.append((turbine, t.isoformat(sep=" "), vibration, round(float(rng.normal(55, 4)), 1),
                             round(float(rng.uniform(40, 60)), 1), (t + timedelta(minutes=5)).isoformat(sep=" ")))
    return rows


def main():
    con = sqlite3.connect("plant.db")
    if "--day4" in sys.argv:
        rng = np.random.RandomState(2)
        con.executemany("INSERT INTO readings (turbine_id, reading_time, vibration_mm_s, temperature_c, power_mw, "
                        "updated_at) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)", readings(rng, 3, 1))
        for reading_id in (10, 20, 30):                         # late corrections to day 1
            con.execute("UPDATE readings SET vibration_mm_s = vibration_mm_s + 0.5, "
                        "updated_at = '2025-06-04 23:00:00' WHERE reading_id = ?", (reading_id,))
    else:
        con.execute("DROP TABLE IF EXISTS readings")
        con.execute("CREATE TABLE readings (reading_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, turbine_id TEXT, reading_time TEXT, "
                    "vibration_mm_s REAL, temperature_c REAL, power_mw REAL, updated_at TEXT)")
        con.executemany("INSERT INTO readings (turbine_id, reading_time, vibration_mm_s, temperature_c, power_mw, "
                        "updated_at) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)", readings(np.random.RandomState(1), 0, 3))
    con.commit()
    print("plant.db readings:", con.execute("SELECT count(*), max(updated_at) FROM readings").fetchone())


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""Lab 1: a zoned data lake on your disk. Raw keeps what arrived, clean is typed, deduplicated and validated,
curated holds features. Ingestion is incremental (a high-watermark) and idempotent."""

import json
import shutil
import sqlite3
from pathlib import Path

import duckdb
import pandas as pd

LAKE = Path("lake")
STATE = LAKE / "_state" / "watermark.json"


def ingest_raw(con):
    """Copy rows changed since the last watermark into the raw zone, as one immutable batch file."""
    watermark = json.loads(STATE.read_text())["updated_at"] if STATE.exists() else "1970-01-01 00:00:00"
    with sqlite3.connect("plant.db") as source:
        batch = pd.read_sql_query("SELECT * FROM readings WHERE updated_at > ? ORDER BY updated_at",
                                  source, params=(watermark,))
    if batch.empty:
        print(f"Raw: no rows changed since {watermark}; nothing written")
        return
    high = batch["updated_at"].max()
    folder = LAKE / "raw" / f"ingest_date={high[:10]}"
    folder.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    name = folder / f"batch_{high.replace(' ', 'T').replace(':', '')}.parquet"
    con.sql("SELECT * FROM batch").write_parquet(str(name))
    # TODO: only now, after the batch file is safely written, save the new watermark:
    #       STATE.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True); STATE.write_text(json.dumps({"updated_at": high}))
    #       Why must this come after the write and not before?
    print(f"Raw: {len(batch)} rows changed since {watermark} -> {name.relative_to(LAKE)}")


def build_clean(con):
    """Rebuild the clean zone from raw: typed, latest version of each reading, validated, partitioned by day."""
    con.execute(f"""
        CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE latest AS
        SELECT reading_id, turbine_id, CAST(reading_time AS TIMESTAMP) AS reading_time,
               vibration_mm_s, temperature_c, power_mw, CAST(updated_at AS TIMESTAMP) AS updated_at,
               CAST(reading_time AS DATE) AS reading_date
        FROM read_parquet('{LAKE}/raw/*/*.parquet')
        -- TODO: keep only the latest version of each reading_id:
        --       QUALIFY row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY reading_id ORDER BY updated_at DESC) = 1
        """)
    valid = "vibration_mm_s BETWEEN 0 AND 50 AND temperature_c BETWEEN -20 AND 120"
    for zone in ("clean", "quarantine"):
        shutil.rmtree(LAKE / zone, ignore_errors=True)
    con.execute(f"COPY (SELECT * FROM latest WHERE {valid}) TO '{LAKE}/clean' "
                "(FORMAT parquet, PARTITION_BY (reading_date))")
    (LAKE / "quarantine").mkdir()
    con.execute(f"COPY (SELECT * FROM latest WHERE NOT ({valid})) TO '{LAKE}/quarantine/rejected.parquet' "
                "(FORMAT parquet)")
    raw = con.sql(f"SELECT count(*) FROM read_parquet('{LAKE}/raw/*/*.parquet')").fetchone()[0]
    kept = con.sql(f"SELECT count(*) FROM read_parquet('{LAKE}/clean/*/*.parquet')").fetchone()[0]
    rejected = con.sql(f"SELECT count(*) FROM '{LAKE}/quarantine/rejected.parquet'").fetchone()[0]
    print(f"Clean: {raw} raw rows -> {kept} clean rows, {rejected} quarantined, "
          f"{raw - kept - rejected} older versions dropped")


def build_curated(con):
    con.execute(f"""
        COPY (SELECT turbine_id, reading_date, round(avg(vibration_mm_s), 3) AS vibration_mean,
                     max(temperature_c) AS temperature_max, round(sum(power_mw) * 0.5, 1) AS energy_mwh
              FROM read_parquet('{LAKE}/clean/*/*.parquet', hive_partitioning=true)
              GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY ALL) TO '{LAKE}/curated_turbine_daily.parquet' (FORMAT parquet)""")
    print("Curated:", con.sql(f"SELECT count(*) FROM '{LAKE}/curated_turbine_daily.parquet'").fetchone()[0],
          "turbine-days;", con.sql(f"""SELECT turbine_id, vibration_mean FROM '{LAKE}/curated_turbine_daily.parquet'
                                    WHERE reading_date = DATE '2025-06-01' AND turbine_id = 'T4'""").fetchone())


def one_day(con, day):
    files = sorted((LAKE / "clean" / f"reading_date={day}").glob("*.parquet"))
    rows = con.sql(f"SELECT count(*) FROM read_parquet('{LAKE}/clean/*/*.parquet', hive_partitioning=true) "
                   f"WHERE reading_date = DATE '{day}'").fetchone()[0]
    print(f"Query for {day}: {rows} rows, from the {len(files)} file(s) in its partition")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    con = duckdb.connect()
    ingest_raw(con)
    build_clean(con)
    build_curated(con)
    one_day(con, "2025-06-02")

modules.title: Lakehouse Architecture
modules.summary: Combine the lake's open storage with a warehouse's guarantees: lakehouse concepts, how Delta Lake and Apache Iceberg work, ACID transactions through a transaction log, and query optimisation.

lessons.title: Lakehouse concepts
objectives: Explain what a lakehouse adds to a data lake
Weigh a lakehouse against a separate lake and warehouse
key_points: A lakehouse adds warehouse features to a data lake: ACID transactions, schema enforcement and evolution, time travel and fast SQL, directly on open files in object storage.
The key component is an open table format, Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg or Apache Hudi: a metadata layer over Parquet files that defines exactly which files make up each version of a table.
One copy of the data can serve BI, data science and ML through several engines, such as Spark, Trino, Flink, DuckDB and cloud warehouses, instead of copying data from a lake into a warehouse.
The medallion layers carry over: bronze, silver and gold become transactional tables rather than folders of loose files.
Table maintenance (compaction, vacuum, statistics) becomes the platform's job, and engines differ in which table-format features they support, so check support before committing to one.

lessons.title: Delta Lake and Apache Iceberg
objectives: Describe how Delta Lake and Apache Iceberg track table versions
Compare their partitioning, updates and time travel
key_points: Delta Lake keeps a transaction log in a _delta_log folder: numbered JSON commits listing the data files added and removed, plus Parquet checkpoints (every 10 commits by default) so readers needn't replay the whole log.

Apache Iceberg keeps metadata as a tree: each table version's metadata file points to a manifest list, which points to manifests listing data files and their column statistics; a catalog holds the pointer to the current metadata file.

Iceberg's hidden partitioning derives partition values from columns with transforms such as day(ts) or bucket(16, id), so queries filter on the column itself and the scheme can evolve without rewriting old data.
Both offer time travel, schema evolution and copy-on-write updates; merge-on-read (delete files in Iceberg, deletion vectors in Delta Lake) makes small updates cheaper at some cost to reads.
Apache Hudi, the third major format, focuses on upserts and incremental processing, with copy-on-write and merge-on-read table types.

lessons.title: ACID transactions on a data lake
objectives: Explain how a transaction log gives atomicity and isolation
Describe optimistic concurrency and its storage requirement
key_points: Atomicity: a commit is one new log entry. Data files are written first and become visible only when the commit lands, so readers see all of a commit's changes or none of them.

Isolation comes from optimistic concurrency: writers read a version, do their work and try to create the next log entry; if another writer got there first the commit fails, and is retried or aborted after a conflict check.
The log needs an atomic create-if-absent (put-if-absent) or a catalog that serialises commits; on storage without one, table formats rely on a catalog or locking service for safe concurrent writers.
A failed or conflicting job leaves only unreferenced data files, which readers never see and vacuum deletes later; nothing half-written is ever part of a version.
Snapshots make time travel cheap: reading an old version replays the log to that point, and the retention period of vacuum decides how far back you can go.

lessons.title: Query optimisation on lakehouse tables
objectives: Use pruning, skipping, clustering and compaction to read less data
Read a query plan to check what a query scans
key_points: Partition pruning skips partitions a filter rules out; data skipping uses each file's min and max column statistics, kept in the table metadata, to skip files whose range can't match.
Clustering puts related rows in the same files so skipping works on more columns: sorting, Z-ordering (Delta Lake's OPTIMIZE ... ZORDER BY), or Delta Lake's newer liquid clustering.
Compaction rewrites many small files into fewer large ones (OPTIMIZE in Delta Lake, rewrite_data_files in Iceberg); streaming writes in particular create small files.
Parquet readers prune columns and push filters down to row groups, so selecting only the columns a query needs and filtering early cuts the bytes read.
Check plans with EXPLAIN or EXPLAIN ANALYZE and keep statistics fresh: the cheapest query is the one that reads the least data.

import shutil, pandas as pd
from deltalake import DeltaTable, write_deltalake
shutil.rmtree("delta_turbines", ignore_errors=True)
for day in ["2025-06-01", "2025-06-02", "2025-06-03"]:
    write_deltalake("delta_turbines", pd.DataFrame({"turbine_id": ["T1", "T2"], "reading_date": [day, day], "vibration_mm_s": [3.1, 2.9]}), mode="append")
dt = DeltaTable("delta_turbines")
print("version", dt.version(), "rows", len(dt.to_pandas()))
dt.delete("turbine_id = 'T2' AND reading_date = '2025-06-02'")
print("after delete: version", dt.version(), "rows", len(dt.to_pandas()))
print("time travel to version 2:", len(DeltaTable("delta_turbines", version=2).to_pandas()), "rows")
print([h["operation"] for h in dt.history()])
import os; print(sorted(os.listdir("delta_turbines/_delta_log")))

modules.title: Streaming Data Patterns
modules.summary: Process events as they happen: stream processing engines and delivery guarantees, event-driven architectures, event-time windows with watermarks and state, and real-time features for ML.

lessons.title: Stream processing engines
objectives: Compare Flink, Spark Structured Streaming, Kafka Streams and Beam
Explain at-most-once, at-least-once and exactly-once processing
key_points: A stream processor runs continuous queries over unbounded event streams, usually reading from a durable log such as Apache Kafka, Amazon Kinesis or Apache Pulsar.

Apache Flink processes events one at a time with event-time semantics, managed state and checkpoints; Spark Structured Streaming runs a series of micro-batches with Spark's batch APIs; Kafka Streams is a library inside your own application.
Apache Beam is a programming model rather than an engine: the same pipeline runs on runners such as Flink, Spark and Google Cloud Dataflow.
At-most-once delivery can lose events and at-least-once can repeat them; exactly-once results need checkpointed state plus idempotent or transactional writes to the sink.
The Lambda architecture keeps a batch layer and a speed layer; the Kappa architecture, described by Jay Kreps in 2014, processes everything as streams and recomputes by replaying the log.

lessons.title: Event-driven architectures
objectives: Distinguish event notification, event-carried state transfer and event sourcing
Design events as contracts that can evolve
key_points: In an event-driven architecture, services publish events, facts that something happened such as ReadingRecorded, and others react, so producers don't need to know who consumes them.

Event notification sends a small message that something changed; event-carried state transfer includes the data consumers need; event sourcing makes the event log the system of record and rebuilds state by replaying it.
Treat events as contracts: a schema registry with Avro, Protobuf or JSON Schema, and compatibility rules, lets producers evolve events without breaking consumers.
Partition streams by a key, such as turbine ID, to keep each key's events in order; there is no ordering across keys.
Expect duplicates and replays: give events unique IDs and make consumers idempotent, and use the outbox pattern to publish events reliably when a database changes.

lessons.title: Windowing, watermarks and state
objectives: Choose between tumbling, sliding and session windows
Explain how watermarks decide when a window is complete
Manage keyed state and late events
key_points: Event time is when something happened; processing time is when the system sees it. Networks and outages deliver events late and out of order, so results that matter should use event time.
Tumbling windows are fixed and don't overlap (every 5 minutes); sliding or hopping windows overlap (10 minutes, every minute); session windows close after a gap with no events.
A watermark is the processor's estimate that no older events are still coming, typically the newest event time seen minus an allowed delay; a window is emitted when the watermark passes its end.
Events arriving after their window has been emitted are late: drop them, send them to a side output, or allow updates for a set lateness, trading completeness against latency.

Keyed state, such as counts or recent readings per turbine, lives in the processor (in memory or an embedded store such as RocksDB) and is checkpointed; give it a time-to-live so it can't grow forever.

lessons.title: Real-time feature engineering
objectives: Design a streaming feature that matches its batch definition
Decide when a feature is worth computing in real time
key_points: Real-time features summarise recent events, such as high-vibration readings in the last 10 minutes; a streaming job computes them and writes them to an online store for low-latency lookups.
Define each feature once and compute it the same way in streaming and in batch training jobs; compare the two regularly, because late events and separate code paths make them diverge.
Point-in-time correctness still applies: training rows need the value the model would have seen at prediction time, which the streaming job's log of emitted values can provide.
Deduplicate by event ID before aggregating, because at-least-once delivery repeats events.
Streaming features add infrastructure and on-call work: use them where freshness measurably improves decisions, and compute slower-changing features in batch.

"""Lab 3: a stream processor in miniature: event time, watermarks, tumbling windows, keyed state and a real-time
feature, checked against the same feature computed in batch with SQL."""

from collections import defaultdict, deque
from datetime import datetime, timedelta

import duckdb
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

WINDOW = timedelta(minutes=5)          # tumbling windows for the dashboard
LATENESS = timedelta(seconds=60)       # how far behind the newest event the watermark trails
FEATURE_SPAN = timedelta(minutes=10)   # real-time feature: high-vibration readings in the last 10 minutes
HIGH = 4.0


def make_events():
    """One hour of readings from six turbines, every 30 s, as they arrive: some late, a few duplicated."""
    rng = np.random.RandomState(4)
    start = datetime(2025, 6, 1, 8, 0)
    rows = []
    for k in range(120):
        for t in ["T1", "T2", "T3", "T4", "T5", "T6"]:
            event_time = start + timedelta(seconds=30 * k)
            base = 3.0 + (1.6 * k / 120 if t == "T4" else 0)        # T4 develops a fault
            delay = rng.choice([rng.uniform(0, 5), rng.uniform(20, 55), rng.uniform(240, 300)], p=[0.93, 0.05, 0.02])
            rows.append({"event_id": f"{t}-{k:03d}", "turbine_id": t, "event_time": event_time,
                         "arrival_time": event_time + timedelta(seconds=float(delay)),
                         "vibration": round(float(rng.normal(base, 0.4)), 2)})
            if rng.rand() < 0.02:                                     # at-least-once delivery: a redelivery
                rows.append(dict(rows[-1], arrival_time=rows[-1]["arrival_time"] + timedelta(seconds=7)))
    return pd.DataFrame(rows).sort_values("arrival_time", kind="stable").reset_index(drop=True)


class Processor:
    def __init__(self):
        self.seen = set()                                  # event ids already processed (for de-duplication)
        self.watermark = datetime.min
        self.windows = defaultdict(lambda: [0, 0.0])        # (turbine, window start) -> [count, sum]
        self.recent = defaultdict(deque)                    # turbine -> (event_time, is_high) in the feature span
        self.closed, self.features = [], {}
        self.duplicates = self.too_late = self.late_accepted = 0

    def process(self, e):
        # TODO: if this event_id was already processed, count it in self.duplicates and return
        self.seen.add(e["event_id"])
        window_start = e["event_time"] - timedelta(minutes=e["event_time"].minute % 5, seconds=e["event_time"].second)
        # TODO: if window_start + WINDOW <= self.watermark, its window has already been emitted:
        #       count the event in self.too_late and return
        if e["event_time"] < self.watermark:
            self.late_accepted += 1
        acc = self.windows[(e["turbine_id"], window_start)]
        acc[0] += 1
        acc[1] += e["vibration"]
        # real-time feature: keep only this turbine's readings inside the span, then count the high ones
        state = self.recent[e["turbine_id"]]
        state.append((e["event_time"], e["vibration"] > HIGH))
        # TODO: evict readings older than e["event_time"] - FEATURE_SPAN from the left of the deque
        self.features[e["event_id"]] = sum(1 for t, high in state if high and t <= e["event_time"])
        # TODO: advance the watermark: the newest event time seen so far minus LATENESS
        for key in [k for k in self.windows if k[1] + WINDOW <= self.watermark]:
            count, total = self.windows.pop(key)
            self.closed.append((key[0], key[1], count, round(total / count, 2)))


def batch_feature(events):
    """The same feature in batch SQL, over every event in event-time order: the answer streaming should match."""
    deduped = events.drop_duplicates("event_id")
    return duckdb.sql("""
        SELECT event_id, sum(CASE WHEN vibration > 4.0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) OVER (
                   PARTITION BY turbine_id ORDER BY event_time
                   RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL 10 MINUTES PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS high_10min
        FROM deduped""").df().set_index("event_id")["high_10min"]


def main():
    events = make_events()
    p = Processor()
    for e in events.to_dict(orient="records"):
        p.process(e)
    print(f"Events delivered: {len(events)}  duplicates dropped: {p.duplicates}  "
          f"late but accepted: {p.late_accepted}  too late, dropped: {p.too_late}")
    print(f"Windows emitted: {len(p.closed)}  still open at the end: {len(p.windows)}")
    t4 = [w for w in p.closed if w[0] == "T4"]
    print(f"T4 first window mean {t4[0][3]}, last emitted window mean {t4[-1][3]}" if t4 else "T4: no windows emitted")
    print(f"State held: {sum(len(q) for q in p.recent.values())} readings across {len(p.recent)} turbines")

    expected = batch_feature(events)
    streamed = pd.Series(p.features)
    common = streamed.index.intersection(expected.index)
    same = (streamed[common] == expected[common]).sum()
    print(f"Real-time feature matches batch SQL for {same} of {len(common)} scored events; "
          f"{len(common) - same} differ because a reading inside their 10 minutes arrived after them")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

hints: A deque's popleft() removes its oldest entry; readings for each turbine arrive mostly in event-time order, so the oldest are at the left.
The watermark only moves forward: max(current watermark, event_time - LATENESS).

modules.title: Hybrid Cloud Architectures
modules.summary: Design ML systems that span on-premises sites and clouds: why organisations go hybrid, keeping data in step between environments, deploying the same model everywhere, and securing it all.

lessons.title: Why hybrid and multi-cloud
objectives: Identify the drivers and costs of hybrid and multi-cloud architectures
Choose where each workload runs
key_points: A hybrid architecture combines on-premises systems with one or more public clouds; multi-cloud uses more than one cloud provider.

Drivers include data that must stay on site or in a country (residency and sovereignty), low latency to plant or factory systems, existing data centres, bursting to cloud GPUs for training, resilience and less dependence on one provider.
The costs are more environments to secure, monitor and staff, data transfer (egress) charges, and services that differ between clouds and pull designs towards the lowest common denominator.

Common patterns: keep data where it's produced and move models to it; train in the cloud on pseudonymised or aggregated data; or run one platform layer, containers and Kubernetes, in every environment.
Record which workloads run where, and why, for each class of data, so placement doesn't drift system by system.

lessons.title: Synchronising data between environments
objectives: Compare replication approaches and their trade-offs
Prove two copies agree with reconciliation
key_points: Replication options include scheduled incremental copies by high-watermark, change data capture streams, object storage replication and database-native replication, trading freshness, source load and complexity.
Watermark-based sync never sees hard deletes; change data capture or soft deletes (tombstone records) are needed to carry deletions.
Upsert by primary key (MERGE, or INSERT OR REPLACE) so rerunning a sync is safe, and apply each batch idempotently.
Reconcile regularly: compare row counts and checksums per partition on both sides and repair only the partitions that differ.
Design for eventual consistency and outages: name the source of truth for each dataset, queue changes while links are down, and monitor replication lag.

lessons.title: Deploying models across clouds
objectives: Package and deploy one model consistently in several environments
Verify that each site runs the registered artefact
key_points: Package models portably: a container image with the serving code and, where it helps, a framework-neutral format such as ONNX, so one artefact runs on site and in any cloud.
Kubernetes gives a common deployment target, and Helm charts or GitOps controllers such as Argo CD and Flux apply the same declarative configuration in every environment.

Identify artefacts by content digest (sha256), never by a mutable tag such as latest, and check at deploy time that what runs matches the registry; signing images and models, for example with Sigstore's cosign, proves their origin.
Keep one model registry as the source of truth, replicate approved versions to each environment, and record promotions and rollbacks centrally.
Give each site health checks and a local fallback model or rule, so predictions continue if the link to the central platform is lost.

lessons.title: Security and compliance across environments
objectives: Apply zero-trust identity, encryption and secrets management across environments
Pseudonymise personal data and check replication plans against policy
key_points: Zero trust: authenticate every user and service, authorise each request with least privilege, and don't trust a network location; federate identity (OpenID Connect, workload identity) instead of copying long-lived keys.

Encrypt in transit (TLS) and at rest with keys in a key management service or hardware security module, and keep secrets in a secrets manager such as HashiCorp Vault or the cloud's own, never in code.
Classify data and enforce rules per class: pseudonymise personal data before it leaves a protected zone; a keyed hash (HMAC) keeps joins possible without exposing the identifier.
Under the GDPR, pseudonymised data is still personal data, because the key can re-identify it, and transfers outside the EEA need a basis such as an adequacy decision or standard contractual clauses.
Write policies as code, for example with Open Policy Agent, check replication and deployment plans against them automatically, and log every access and change centrally for audit.

"""Lab 4: keep a cloud copy in step with an on-premises database, prove it with reconciliation, pseudonymise
personal data before it leaves, check a replication plan against policy, and check deployed model digests."""

import hashlib
import hmac
import json
import sqlite3
from pathlib import Path

import duckdb
import pandas as pd

SECRET = b"rotate-me-and-keep-me-in-a-vault"     # in production: from a secrets manager, never in code
CLOUD = Path("cloud")


def make_onprem():
    con = sqlite3.connect("onprem.db")
    con.executescript("""
        DROP TABLE IF EXISTS readings; DROP TABLE IF EXISTS operators;
        CREATE TABLE readings (reading_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, plant_id TEXT, reading_time TEXT,
                               vibration_mm_s REAL, updated_at TEXT);
        CREATE TABLE operators (operator_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, email TEXT, phone TEXT, plant_id TEXT);""")
    rows = [(i, "P1" if i % 2 else "P2", f"2025-06-0{1 + (i - 1) // 100} {i % 24:02d}:00:00",
             round(3 + (i % 7) * 0.1, 2), f"2025-06-0{1 + (i - 1) // 100} {i % 24:02d}:05:00") for i in range(1, 301)]
    con.executemany("INSERT INTO readings VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?)", rows)
    con.executemany("INSERT INTO operators VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?)", [
        ("OP1", "Farrukh Nazarov", "f.nazarov@plant.example", "+992 37 000 0001", "P1"),
        ("OP2", "Madina Rahimova", "m.rahimova@plant.example", "+992 37 000 0002", "P2")])
    con.commit()
    return con


def sync(onprem, cloud):
    """Incremental sync with a high-watermark, merged into the cloud table by primary key (an upsert)."""
    cloud.execute("CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS readings (reading_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, plant_id VARCHAR, "
                  "reading_time VARCHAR, vibration_mm_s DOUBLE, updated_at VARCHAR)")
    cloud.execute("CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS sync_state (name VARCHAR PRIMARY KEY, watermark VARCHAR)")
    row = cloud.execute("SELECT watermark FROM sync_state WHERE name = 'readings'").fetchone()
    watermark = row[0] if row else "1970-01-01"
    changed = pd.read_sql_query("SELECT * FROM readings WHERE updated_at > ?", onprem, params=(watermark,))
    if len(changed):
        # TODO: upsert the changed rows into the cloud table (INSERT OR REPLACE INTO readings SELECT * FROM changed),
        #       then save the new watermark: INSERT OR REPLACE INTO sync_state VALUES ('readings', <max updated_at>)
        pass
    print(f"Sync: {len(changed)} changed rows since {watermark}")


def reconcile(onprem, cloud):
    """Compare per-day counts and a checksum on both sides; any difference names the days to repair."""
    query = ("SELECT substr(reading_time, 1, 10) AS day, count(*) AS n, "
             "sum(CAST(round(vibration_mm_s * 100) AS INTEGER)) AS checksum FROM readings GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1")
    source = pd.read_sql_query(query, onprem).set_index("day")
    target = cloud.sql(query).df().set_index("day")
    diff = source.compare(target.reindex(source.index)) if len(source) == len(target) else source
    bad = sorted(set(diff.index))
    print("Reconciliation:", "in sync" if not bad else f"mismatch on {bad}",
          f"({int(source['n'].sum())} rows on-premises, {int(target['n'].sum())} in the cloud)")


def pseudonymise(operators):
    """Keep what analytics needs, replace what identifies a person: a keyed hash keeps joins possible
    without revealing the email, and only someone with the key could recompute it."""
    out = operators[["operator_id", "plant_id"]].copy()
    # TODO: a keyed hash of each lower-cased email: hmac.new(SECRET, email.lower().encode(), hashlib.sha256),
    #       keeping the first 16 hex characters of its hexdigest()
    out["email_token"] = "TODO"
    out["phone_country"] = operators["phone"].str.split().str[0]
    return out


def check_plan(plan, policy):
    violations = []
    for step in plan:
        meta = policy["datasets"][step["dataset"]]
        region = policy["regions"][step["to"]]
        # TODO rule 1: eu-resident datasets may go only to "eu" or "on-premises" regions
        # TODO rule 2: columns classified "pii" may not leave "on-premises" un-pseudonymised
        pass
    return violations


def digest(path):
    return "sha256:" + hashlib.sha256(Path(path).read_bytes()).hexdigest()


def main():
    CLOUD.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    (CLOUD / "warehouse.duckdb").unlink(missing_ok=True)
    onprem, cloud = make_onprem(), duckdb.connect(str(CLOUD / "warehouse.duckdb"))
    sync(onprem, cloud)
    reconcile(onprem, cloud)

    onprem.execute("UPDATE readings SET vibration_mm_s = 9.9, updated_at = '2025-06-04 10:00:00' WHERE reading_id = 42")
    onprem.execute("INSERT INTO readings VALUES (301, 'P1', '2025-06-04 09:00:00', 3.3, '2025-06-04 09:05:00')")
    onprem.commit()
    sync(onprem, cloud)
    reconcile(onprem, cloud)

    onprem.execute("DELETE FROM readings WHERE reading_id = 7")      # a hard delete leaves no updated_at behind
    onprem.commit()
    sync(onprem, cloud)
    reconcile(onprem, cloud)

    operators = pd.read_sql_query("SELECT * FROM operators", onprem)
    print("Pseudonymised operators:", pseudonymise(operators).to_dict(orient="records")[0])

    policy = json.loads(Path("data_policy.json").read_text())
    plan = [{"dataset": "readings", "to": "cloud-eu-west", "columns": ["reading_id", "plant_id", "vibration_mm_s"]},
            {"dataset": "operators", "to": "cloud-eu-west", "columns": ["operator_id", "email", "plant_id"]},
            {"dataset": "readings", "to": "cloud-us-east", "columns": ["reading_id", "vibration_mm_s"]}]
    for v in check_plan(plan, policy):
        print("Policy violation:", v)

    Path("model.bin").write_bytes(b"turbine-fault-model v7 weights")
    Path("model_patched.bin").write_bytes(b"turbine-fault-model v7 weights, hot-fixed on site")
    registry = {"turbine-fault": {"version": 7, "digest": digest("model.bin")}}
    for site, artefact in [("onprem-dushanbe", "model.bin"), ("cloud-eu-west", "model_patched.bin")]:
        ok = digest(artefact) == registry["turbine-fault"]["digest"]
        print(f"Deployment {site}: {'matches the registry' if ok else 'DIGEST MISMATCH: not the registered model'}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

modules.title: Enterprise MLOps
modules.summary: Run ML at enterprise scale: maturity models, automated CI, CD and continuous training pipelines, model governance with registries, model cards and approvals, and safe promotion of retrained models.

lessons.title: MLOps maturity models
objectives: Describe Google's and Microsoft's MLOps maturity levels
Assess an organisation's maturity and choose the next step
key_points: Maturity models describe how automated and governed ML delivery is, so a team can see where it stands and what to improve next.
Google Cloud's MLOps guidance describes level 0 (manual, script-driven), level 1 (ML pipeline automation with continuous training) and level 2 (CI/CD automation of the pipelines themselves).

Microsoft's MLOps maturity model has five levels: 0, no MLOps; 1, DevOps but no MLOps; 2, automated training; 3, automated model deployment; and 4, full MLOps automated operations, including retraining.
Assess each dimension separately (data management, experiment tracking, training, deployment, monitoring, governance) and raise the weakest one that blocks the most value.
Higher isn't always better: automate what changes often or fails expensively; a low-risk model retrained twice a year may not need continuous training.

lessons.title: Automated pipelines: CI, CD and continuous training
objectives: Define CI, CD and CT for ML systems
Compare a challenger with a champion fairly
key_points: Continuous integration for ML tests code, data and models: unit tests for feature code, data validation (schema, ranges, freshness), and minimum-quality checks on trained models.
Continuous delivery moves the training pipeline and the serving system through development, staging and production with the same automation.
Continuous training retrains on new data on a schedule or when triggered by drift, new labels or falling performance, and evaluates the challenger before anything is promoted.
Compare challenger and champion on the same recent, held-out data with the same metrics, including per-segment ones, so a lucky split doesn't decide.
Keep pipelines reproducible: version code, data snapshots, configuration and environment images, and record lineage from data to deployed model.

lessons.title: Model governance
objectives: Describe the records and controls of model governance
Tier models by risk and apply segregation of duties
key_points: Governance makes ML decisions accountable: who built a model, on what data, how it was tested, who approved it, where it runs and when it changed.
A model registry stores each version with metrics, lineage, stage (staging, production, archived) and approvals; an append-only audit log records every change.
Model cards (Mitchell and colleagues, 2019) document intended use, training data, evaluation by group, limitations and owners; a deployment gate can refuse a model whose card is incomplete.
Tier models by risk: high-risk models, such as those affecting safety, credit or employment, need stricter review, segregation of duties (the approver isn't the author) and closer monitoring.

Frameworks to align with include the NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0, 2023), ISO/IEC 42001 for AI management systems, the EU AI Act's duties for high-risk systems, and, in banking, model risk guidance such as the US SR 11-7.

lessons.title: Continuous training and safe promotion
objectives: Choose retraining triggers
Design a promotion gate and a gradual release
key_points: Retraining triggers include a schedule, enough new labelled data, input drift (such as a population stability index over 0.25) and a drop in live performance once labels arrive.
A promotion gate checks explicit rules: a minimum improvement over the champion, no segment made worse, fairness gaps within limits, documentation complete, and approvals in place.
Release the winner gradually, in shadow or as a canary, keep the champion ready for rollback, and record why each model was promoted or rejected.
Retraining alone doesn't fix everything: a new population may need new features, such as terms for a new turbine type, new labels or a separate model, so review what changed, not just the score.
Watch for feedback loops, where a model's decisions change the data it is later trained on, such as inspections preventing the very faults the model predicts.

"""Lab 5: continuous training with governance. A trigger decides when to retrain, a challenger is trained and
compared with the champion on the same recent data, a gate checks performance, fairness, documentation and
approval, and every decision lands in an audit log of a small registry."""

import json
import sqlite3
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import recall_score, roc_auc_score
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, StandardScaler

FEATURES = ["vibration_mean", "temperature_max", "load_factor", "days_since_service", "turbine_type", "region"]
TYPE_B_TERMS = ["b_vibration", "b_temperature"]       # the challenger's new features: type-B-specific slopes
REQUIRED_CARD_FIELDS = ["owner", "intended_use", "training_data", "metrics", "limitations", "risk_tier"]


def make_data():
    """Four months of daily turbine records; in month 4 a new turbine type, B, becomes common."""
    rng = np.random.RandomState(6)
    parts = []
    for month in range(1, 5):
        n = 900
        turbine_type = rng.choice(["A", "B"], n, p=[0.95, 0.05] if month < 4 else [0.5, 0.5])
        vibration = np.round(rng.normal(3.0, 0.5, n) + (turbine_type == "B") * 0.9, 2)
        temperature = np.round(rng.normal(60, 6, n), 1)
        load = np.round(rng.uniform(0.3, 1.0, n), 2)
        days = rng.randint(0, 180, n)
        region = rng.choice(["north", "south"], n)
        is_b = turbine_type == "B"
        logit = np.where(is_b, -2.6 + 0.2 * (vibration - 3.9) + 0.18 * (temperature - 60),
                         -3.4 + 1.8 * (vibration - 3.0) + 0.03 * (temperature - 60)) + 1.0 * load + 0.012 * days
        fault = (rng.rand(n) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-logit))).astype(int)
        parts.append(pd.DataFrame({"month": month, "vibration_mean": vibration, "temperature_max": temperature,
                                   "load_factor": load, "days_since_service": days, "turbine_type": turbine_type,
                                   "region": region, "fault_7d": fault}))
    data = pd.concat(parts, ignore_index=True)
    b = data["turbine_type"] == "B"
    data["b_vibration"] = np.where(b, data["vibration_mean"] - 3.9, 0.0)
    data["b_temperature"] = np.where(b, data["temperature_max"] - 60, 0.0)
    return data


def psi(reference, live, bins=10):
    edges = np.unique(np.quantile(reference, np.linspace(0, 1, bins + 1)))
    edges[0], edges[-1] = -np.inf, np.inf
    ref = np.clip(np.histogram(reference, edges)[0] / len(reference), 1e-4, None)
    cur = np.clip(np.histogram(live, edges)[0] / len(live), 1e-4, None)
    return float(np.sum((cur - ref) * np.log(cur / ref)))


def train(data, extra=()):
    numeric = FEATURES[:4] + list(extra)
    prep = ColumnTransformer([("num", StandardScaler(), numeric),
                              ("cat", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"), ["turbine_type", "region"])])
    model = make_pipeline(prep, LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))
    return model.fit(data[numeric + ["turbine_type", "region"]], data["fault_7d"])


def evaluate(model, data, threshold=0.25):
    p = model.predict_proba(data[list(model.feature_names_in_)])[:, 1]
    recalls = {r: recall_score(data["fault_7d"][data["region"] == r], p[data["region"] == r] >= threshold)
               for r in ["north", "south"]}
    return {"auc": round(roc_auc_score(data["fault_7d"], p), 3),
            "recall_by_region": {r: round(v, 3) for r, v in recalls.items()},
            "recall_gap": round(max(recalls.values()) - min(recalls.values()), 3)}


class Registry:
    def __init__(self, path="registry.db"):
        Path(path).unlink(missing_ok=True)
        self.db = sqlite3.connect(path)
        self.db.executescript("""
            CREATE TABLE models (name TEXT, version INTEGER, stage TEXT, metrics TEXT, author TEXT,
                                 PRIMARY KEY (name, version));
            CREATE TABLE audit (seq INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT, event TEXT, detail TEXT);""")

    def log(self, event, detail):
        self.db.execute("INSERT INTO audit (event, detail) VALUES (?, ?)", (event, json.dumps(detail)))

    def register(self, name, version, stage, metrics, author):
        self.db.execute("INSERT INTO models VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?)", (name, version, stage, json.dumps(metrics), author))
        self.log("registered", {"model": name, "version": version, "stage": stage})

    def set_stage(self, name, version, stage):
        self.db.execute("UPDATE models SET stage = ? WHERE name = ? AND version = ?", (stage, name, version))
        self.log("stage changed", {"model": name, "version": version, "stage": stage})


def gate(champion, challenger, card, author, approver):
    # TODO: return a dictionary of check name -> True/False:
    #   "beats champion by 0.005 AUC"                 challenger AUC minus champion AUC is at least 0.005
    #   "no region loses recall"                      no region's recall falls by more than 0.02
    #   "recall gap between regions <= 0.10"          the challenger's recall_gap
    #   "model card complete"                         every field in REQUIRED_CARD_FIELDS is filled in
    #   "approved by someone other than the author"   needed when the card's risk_tier is "high"
    return {"beats champion by 0.005 AUC": challenger["auc"] > champion["auc"]}


def main():
    data = make_data()
    reference, recent = data[data["month"] <= 3], data[data["month"] == 4]
    registry = Registry()

    champion_model = train(reference[reference["month"] <= 2])
    registry.register("turbine-fault", 1, "Production", evaluate(champion_model, reference[reference["month"] == 3]),
                      "amina")

    drift = {c: round(psi(reference[c], recent[c]), 3) for c in ["vibration_mean", "temperature_max", "load_factor"]}
    reasons = [f"PSI {c} {v}" for c, v in drift.items() if v > 0.25]
    print(f"Trigger check: drift {drift}; new labelled rows {len(recent)}")
    if not reasons:
        print("No retraining needed")
        return
    registry.log("retraining triggered", {"reasons": reasons})
    print("Retraining triggered by:", reasons)

    holdout = recent.sample(frac=0.4, random_state=0)                      # the latest month, held out
    train_rows = pd.concat([reference, recent.drop(holdout.index)])
    challenger_model = train(train_rows, extra=TYPE_B_TERMS)
    champion, challenger = evaluate(champion_model, holdout), evaluate(challenger_model, holdout)
    print(f"Champion v1 on recent data:   {champion}")
    print(f"Challenger v2 on recent data: {challenger}")
    registry.register("turbine-fault", 2, "Staging", challenger, "amina")

    card = json.loads(Path("model_card_v2.json").read_text())
    for approver in [None, "amina", "davron"]:
        checks = gate(champion, challenger, card, author="amina", approver=approver)
        failed = [name for name, ok in checks.items() if not ok]
        registry.log("gate evaluated", {"approver": approver, "failed": failed})
        print(f"Gate with approver {approver!r}: {'PASS' if not failed else 'FAIL ' + str(failed)}")
        if not failed:
            registry.set_stage("turbine-fault", 1, "Archived")
            registry.set_stage("turbine-fault", 2, "Production")
            break
    print("Registry:", registry.db.execute("SELECT version, stage FROM models ORDER BY version").fetchall())
    print("Audit log:", [e for (e,) in registry.db.execute("SELECT event FROM audit ORDER BY seq")])


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

{
  "model": "turbine-fault",
  "version": 2,
  "owner": "reliability-ml team",
  "intended_use": "Rank turbines by risk of a fault in the next 7 days, to schedule inspections. Not for automatic shutdowns.",
  "training_data": "Daily turbine features, months 1-4 (point-in-time joined); data snapshot hash in the registry",
  "metrics": "ROC AUC and recall at the inspection threshold, overall and per region, on the latest month",
  "limitations": "Trained on two turbine types; new types need fresh evaluation before use.",
  "risk_tier": "high"
}

hints: all(card.get(f) for f in REQUIRED_CARD_FIELDS) is False when any field is missing or empty.
For a high-risk card, the approval check needs an approver who isn't None and isn't the author.

project.title: Design a cloud-agnostic lakehouse with streaming and MLOps
project.brief: A hydropower company runs plants in two countries. Turbine sensors stream readings every few seconds, the maintenance system keeps work orders in an on-premises database, and operators' personal data must stay in its country of origin. The company wants a lakehouse that serves dashboards, data science and a fault-prediction model, on-premises and in a cloud region, without being tied to one vendor. Design it: an architecture diagram (start from the Mermaid diagram in architecture_template.md), the eight sections of the architecture document, and at least five architecture decision records (adr_template.md) for the choices that matter most, such as the table format, the stream processor, where training runs, how personal data is protected and the promotion gate. Then build a walking skeleton that runs locally, reusing and extending your labs: bronze, silver and gold tables with incremental ingestion, a streaming feature written to an online store (SQLite is enough) and to the offline store, a point-in-time training set, training with a governed promotion into a registry, and a reconciliation report between two environments.
deliverables: An architecture diagram covering sources, batch and streaming paths, the table format and catalog, online and offline feature stores, training, registry and serving in both environments
The architecture document, all eight sections
At least five ADRs, each with context, decision, alternatives and consequences
A walking skeleton: ingestion into bronze, silver and gold tables, a streaming feature job writing to online and offline stores, and a point-in-time training set
A training and promotion step with a registry, model card, gate and audit log
A reconciliation report showing the on-premises and cloud copies agree, and a policy check of your replication plan
A README with run instructions and a short cost, risk and operations section

rubric.description: The diagram and document show batch and streaming paths, storage, catalog, feature stores, training, registry and serving, consistent with the stated constraints.

rubric.name: Decision records
rubric.description: At least five ADRs weigh real alternatives with consequences, including the table format and where training and personal data live.

rubric.name: Data platform skeleton
rubric.description: Ingestion is incremental and idempotent, tables are transactional or versioned, and the batch and streaming features agree on the same definition.

rubric.name: Hybrid, security and compliance
rubric.description: Residency and PII rules are enforced in code, replication is reconciled, and identity, encryption, secrets and audit are designed for both environments.

rubric.name: MLOps and governance
rubric.description: Training uses a point-in-time set, a gate checks performance, segments, documentation and approval, and every promotion is in an audit log with a rollback path.

rubric.name: Clarity and operability
rubric.description: The README runs end to end, and costs, risks and day-two operations are considered.
